transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-05-22
Time: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen; Priya Raman; Samir Patel; Laura Gomez; Ben Ortiz

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex from Redwood, and with me is Priya our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Samir Patel: Good, Alex. Thanks. Busy week but excited to get this down.
[00:09] Laura Gomez: Hi, thanks for setting this up. We want to make sure we cover compliance and network topology first.
[00:14] Alex Chen: Totally, that's the plan. Quick agenda: we want to understand your current infra, constraints (regions, egress, MPLS), who needs access, and success criteria. Then we'll sketch options: hosted vs dedicated vs private and deep-dive on private — VPC peering, Transit GW, private endpoints.
[00:27] Ben Ortiz: Sounds good. I'll try to jump in with details.

[00:40] Priya Raman: Maybe I can start by asking about your baseline: what cloud providers and regions do you run in today?
[00:44] Samir Patel: We're multi-cloud. Primary is AWS — us-east-1 and eu-west-1 for production, GCP for some batch workloads in europe-west2. We have a requirement that EU customer data must stay in eu-west-1 or europe-west2 depending on contract.
[00:58] Priya Raman: Got it. Region gating is common. Do you need Redwood instances physically in eu-west-1 for inference, or will routing via private link to a US region be acceptable?
[01:09] Laura Gomez: We need inference to run in the EU for EU-resident customers. Legal is strict on that. And audit logs must live in their region or be under our KMS.
[01:20] Alex Chen: Understood. For Private deployments we can run control plane in your VPC / private control plane, and you can pin model hosts in eu-west-1. We'll need to discuss availability zones and spread to meet your SLA.

[01:33] Ben Ortiz: What's the footprint for a minimal private fabric? We want low-latency for synchronous calls — typically under 200ms P95 — and we have spikes. What's the typical network architecture?
[01:44] Priya Raman: In AWS we usually recommend either VPC peering for single-account setups or a Transit Gateway for hub-and-spoke when you have multiple VPCs or cross-account peering. PrivateLink (AWS PrivateLink / Interface endpoints) is often used for control-plane connectivity or for minimizing cross-AZ egress costs.
[01:58] Samir Patel: We're a bit hybrid — multiple AWS accounts and an on-prem colo connected by Direct Connect. Do you support Direct Connect + VGW + Transit Gateway patterns?
[02:07] Alex Chen: Yes, Redwood's Private supports peering, Transit Gateway, and on-prem via Direct Connect. For latency-critical paths, we usually colocate inference in the same AZ when possible. For multi-account environments we prefer Transit Gateway because it simplifies route management and centralizes egress controls.

[02:22] Laura Gomez: How do you handle DNS and private endpoints? We use Route 53 private hosted zones today, and we need TLS + mTLS for internal services.
[02:30] Priya Raman: PrivateLink endpoints expose a private ENI in your VPC and you can use Route 53 private zones to resolve to those endpoints. For TLS, we recommend customer-managed certs and mutual TLS where needed; Redwood can integrate with your KMS/HSM for key handling. Note: sometimes the auto-gen certs confuse internal tooling so we prefer bringing certs or using ACM where possible.

[02:47] Ben Ortiz: There's also IP planning. We've got tight CIDR space. How many IPs do you typically need for private workers / inference nodes?
[02:54] Priya Raman: Minimal deployments can run in a small subnet but each GPU node needs an ENI. For scaling we suggest /22 per deployment as a starting point but we can tune that. If you're tight, we can do NAT+egress through a smaller set of IPs, but that affects SNI and some vendor allowlists.
[03:09] Samir Patel: We have a /20 across the org, but a lot is used. We need guidance.

[03:18] Alex Chen: We'll send an IP planning doc. One callout: if you want predictable egress IPs for firewall allowlisting, you should route egress via a NAT gateway or private egress appliance in a controlled AZ — Redwood can support that pattern.

[03:35] Laura Gomez: Security-wise, we need SOC2 and ISO artifacts, SAML SSO integration for RBAC, audit logs forwarded to our SIEM (Splunk), and key management in our KMS. Is that supported?
[03:46] Priya Raman: Yes. For Private we offer audit logs and can stream them to your S3 bucket or direct to SIEM via our log collector. SSO via SAML/SCIM is supported for user provisioning. For KMS, we integrate with AWS KMS and customer-managed keys; for HSM we can discuss a dedicated signing path.

[04:02] Ben Ortiz: How about model caching and KV cache across nodes — like if we run canary or A/B rollouts, what's the impact on intra-VPC traffic?
[04:11] Priya Raman: The runtime maintains local KV caches per node for performance; cross-node sync is minimized. If you want global prefix cache, that adds intra-VPC traffic but reduces model compute. We can show you tradeoffs and estimate bytes/sec for your workload.

[04:27] Samir Patel: We plan to run a mix of large models and smaller quantized variants. Can you route low-priority requests to cheaper quantized instances?
[04:36] Alex Chen: Yes — Smart routing and model variants is part of Redwood. For Private you can set policies to route by priority, latency SLO, or cost. We'll discuss cost estimates in the pricing doc.

[04:48] Laura Gomez: For compliance, logs must be immutable and retained for 365 days. Can you commit to that or will we need to implement retention on our side?
[04:55] Priya Raman: We can push logs to your S3 with immutable object lock if you enable it; retention policy then is yours to enforce. Redwood retains minimal control-plane records as per contract; for full audit trail we recommend log forwarding to your bucket.

[05:12] Ben Ortiz: Network egress: we have strict egress filters outbound to the internet. If some model pulls artifacts or downloads tokenizer libraries, how does that work?
[05:22] Alex Chen: For Private you can whitelist Redwood's image registry endpoints or host a local mirror. For models we can pre-stage weights in your environment so there's no outbound traffic during inference.

[05:36] Samir Patel: Can you run in an air-gapped fashion? Not fully, but some customers require no external control plane.
[05:42] Priya Raman: We support an option where the control plane is handed over to you — Private with customer-managed control plane. That approach minimizes external dependencies but increases the operational footprint.

[05:55] Laura Gomez: What's the upgrade story? Patching, model upgrades, and security patches — who handles that in Private?
[06:02] Priya Raman: There are two models: managed Private where Redwood handles patching and rollouts via your approvals, and self-managed where you run the operator and apply upgrades. For enterprise customers we typically run managed Private with canary rollouts and a single-click pause.

[06:17] Ben Ortiz: Back to networking: Do you support AWS Transit Gateway route tables per environment? We use multiple route tables to isolate environments.
[06:25] Priya Raman: Yes, we can attach to specific TGW route tables. Redwood's recommended pattern is to use a dedicated route table for the inference fabric and enforce egress controls via NACLs and security groups.

[06:39] Alex Chen: Quick check — any hard blockers that would make Redwood a no-go?
[06:43] Laura Gomez: If we can't keep logs within region under our KMS, that's a blocker. Also, we need guaranteed pen-tests and pre-onboarding security questionnaires answered.
[06:55] Alex Chen: That's fair. We'll share SOC2/ISO artifacts and a filled security questionnaire. We can also schedule a pen-test coordination call.

[07:06] Samir Patel: A practical question: how do we connect our on-prem via Direct Connect? We use a private VIF into a Transit Gateway. We want inference nodes to be accessible from on-prem with low hop count.
[07:18] Priya Raman: Attach Redwood's VPC to your TGW, and we can announce routes for the inference subnets. For public egress we can route via your NAT or via Redwood's managed egress depending on the model. For low hop count, colocating nodes in the same AZ as the DX endpoint and leveraging local peering helps.

[07:36] Ben Ortiz: For failover across regions — say eu-west-1 to us-east-1 — do you support cross-region replication of model cache or is it cold start?
[07:45] Priya Raman: We don't replicate KV cache across regions by default — that's expensive. We rely on stable routing and warm pools in each region. For disaster recovery we suggest active-passive with pre-warmed instances in secondary region.

[07:58] Laura Gomez: Can we limit which models are allowed in which region? Example: EU models in eu-west-1 only.
[08:04] Alex Chen: Yes, deployment policies let you pin model versions and model families to regions. We can enforce region restrictions and automatic fallback to compatible family within the same region.

[08:16] Samir Patel: Ops question: how are IPs presented to our firewall team? They need a small static set.
[08:22] Priya Raman: We present either ENIs (if the nodes live in your VPC) or a small set of egress NAT IPs for outbound traffic that you can allowlist. For inbound you control the security groups.

[08:34] Ben Ortiz: Are there any gotchas with cross-account peering and permissions? We have separate accounts for prod, stage, and infra.
[08:41] Priya Raman: Cross-account peering requires route propagation and IAM roles for deployment. We typically recommend using TGW with resource-based policies to simplify cross-account access.

[08:52] Alex Chen: Let's talk about bandwidth and throughput — do you have an estimate of RPS and average prompt size?
[08:58] Ben Ortiz: For phase 1 we expect 120 RPS with average 60 tokens per request, but for scheduled jobs we can burst to 800 RPS for short windows.
[09:10] Priya Raman: Good to know. We'll run throughput estimates and advise on GPU sizing. Batching and KV cache will help with cost. Also, autoscaling policies matter: scale on queue depth or CPU/GPU utilization.

[09:22] Samir Patel: If we do a pilot, what's the minimum duration and what telemetry do you need?
[09:27] Alex Chen: We typically run an 8–12 week pilot to tune caching and batching and to validate SLOs. For telemetry: sample prompts, token distributions, latency traces, and error rates. We'll sign an NDA for actual data.

[09:40] Laura Gomez: About encryption in transit and at rest — do you support mTLS for client-to-proxy and server-to-server?
[09:47] Priya Raman: Yes, mTLS supported. For KMS, we can use customer-managed keys in AWS KMS or external HSM through standard APIs.

[09:56] Ben Ortiz: One more thing: do you have any limitations with GCP Private Service Connect vs AWS PrivateLink?
[10:03] Priya Raman: GCP's Private Service Connect is similar in concept. We support PSC for GCP and PrivateLink for AWS. Implementation details differ (forwarding rules vs interface endpoints) but the net effect is a private, VPC-local endpoint. We'll provide templates for both.

[10:18] Alex Chen: Quick pause — any questions so far?
[10:21] Samir Patel: Not yet, go on.

[10:30] Priya Raman: Let's run through a recommended design for Mentis: hub Transit Gateway in prod account in eu-west-1, attach Redwood inference VPC as a spoke via TGW attachment; create private endpoints for control plane via PrivateLink; use NAT with known egress IPs for outbound allowlist; pre-stage models in region and enforce KMS key policies per-region.
[10:52] Ben Ortiz: That sounds right. For the Transit GW route table we'll want to block internet egress except through our central firewall.
[10:58] Priya Raman: Totally doable; route tables and NACLs will enforce that. We can also set up VPC Flow logs for monitoring.

[11:08] Laura Gomez: We need an SLA of 99.9% for inference latency and availability for prod. Can Redwood commit to that for Private?
[11:16] Alex Chen: For Dedicated we offer SLA-backed options; for Private we can include SLAs in the contract depending on the deployment model and capacity commitments. If you reserve capacity (Committed Dedicated) we can hit strict SLAs.

[11:30] Samir Patel: Cost: can we get a rough delta between Dedicated reserved capacity and Private? We're comparing management overhead vs unit cost.
[11:38] Alex Chen: High-level: Dedicated reserved pools are cheaper per-token for large, steady workloads; Private adds operational cost but gives you full data control and network isolation. We'll send a back-of-envelope based on your RPS numbers.

[11:50] Ben Ortiz: Are there any IPAM or ENI limits we should watch out for on AWS? We hit ENI limits before.
[11:56] Priya Raman: Yes, instance ENI limits can bite you. We'll size nodes and pick instance types to avoid hitting ENI limits; alternatives are using secondary ENIs or single larger instances. We'll include instance sizing guidance.

[12:08] Laura Gomez: On certification — do you provide an ATO pack or anything for FedRAMP-like customers? Not now, but planning ahead.
[12:15] Alex Chen: We don't have FedRAMP out-of-the-box yet, but we can provide artifacts and a roadmap. For EU regulated customers we have data residency and encryption artifacts.

[12:26] Samir Patel: Regarding network observability, can Redwood export traces to Jaeger or OpenTelemetry?
[12:33] Priya Raman: Yes, we support OpenTelemetry and can stream traces to your backend. We also provide per-route token-level cost breakdowns in the Console.

[12:44] Ben Ortiz: For the pilot, what's the minimal environment you need within our VPCs?
[12:50] Priya Raman: Minimal: one subnet per AZ for inference, security groups, a role for deployment, and a bucket for logs. We'll provide a Terraform module to bootstrap.

[13:00] Alex Chen: Let's capture blockers: Laura will send compliance constraints list; Ben will share VPC diagram; Redwood will send security pack and an IP planning doc; Priya will prepare a TGW + PrivateLink reference design. Any other items?
[13:15] Laura Gomez: Also need an item for data retention and log immutability confirmation.

[13:22] Samir Patel: Timing: we want a pilot in Q3, ideally starting July. Is that feasible?
[13:27] Alex Chen: Yes, Q3 start is reasonable. We'll aim to have the design and pricing in early June so you can schedule procurement.

[13:36] Ben Ortiz: Quick clarification — you mentioned pre-staging models. Do you support model registry integration (e.g., MLflow or internal registry)?
[13:44] Priya Raman: We have connectors for common registries and can pull artifacts from your private registry. We can also S3-stage artifacts.

[13:52] Laura Gomez: One more security question: will the node images be scanned? We have a vulnerability policy.
[13:57] Priya Raman: Nodes are scanned; Redwood can provide SBOMs and vulnerability scan results upon request. If you want to run your own scanner, we can provide access to images in your account or a registry mirror.

[14:09] Alex Chen: We're at about 45 minutes — wanted to recap and confirm next steps.
[14:14] Priya Raman: Recap: Redwood to send security pack (SOC2/ISO), IP planning doc, TGW/PrivateLink reference design, and pricing for Dedicated vs Private. Mentis to send VPC diagram, list of regulated regions/customers, and confirm pilot timeline (July).
[14:28] Samir Patel: Correct. We'll try to get the VPC diagram and constraints by end of next week.
[14:32] Laura Gomez: We'll compile the compliance list and send it with the procurement team.

[14:40] Alex Chen: Great. I'll follow up with an email and attach the security artifacts. Priya will run the design doc and schedule the technical deep-dive.
[14:48] Ben Ortiz: Thanks everyone. This was helpful.
[14:50] Samir Patel: Thanks.
[14:51] Laura Gomez: Thanks, bye.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcript fidelity: occasional mis-heard product names and abbreviations possible (e.g., PrivateLink vs Private Link). Some timestamps approximate.
